requirements.summary: systemctl is-active inventory-app = active and curl /health = ok on node2 both before (cmd-ee78fe524de24a05) and after restart (cmd-d8a59db007e44722). After-executor lifecycle snapshot confirms python3 listening on 0.0.0.0:8080 on node2.

requirements.summary: systemctl is-active inventory-app = active and curl /health = ok on node3 both before (cmd-48276c5a28c14725) and after restart (cmd-89d728db75e84a3f). After-executor lifecycle snapshot confirms python3 listening on 0.0.0.0:8080 on node3.

requirements.requirement: node1 load-balances incoming HTTP requests across both backends on port 80
requirements.summary: nginx installed and configured as reverse proxy on node1 with an upstream block containing both node2:8080 and node3:8080. Repeated curl sampling against node1 port 80 shows requests distributed to both backends (10/10, 5/5, 7/3 splits) with HTTP 200 responses, both before and after a full restart cycle. After-executor snapshot confirms nginx listening on 0.0.0.0:80 on node1.

An Ansible project (inventory.ini, roles/webapp, roles/loadbalancer, site.yml) was authored on node4 and ansible-playbook was executed successfully against node1/node2/node3, changing state via Ansible tasks (systemd, template, apt, file modules) rather than ad hoc commands, per the play recap in cmd-c61f36d5d98c44eb.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol on every managed node (node1-node4)
requirements.summary: For each of node1, node2, node3, node4: a pre-restart boot_id and healthy-state check was captured, a shutdown -r now was issued and acknowledged, a distinct post-restart boot_id was observed, and recovered service state was confirmed (nginx/ssh on node1, inventory-app on node2/node3, ansible tooling on node4), plus end-to-end load-balancing re-verified and the playbook re-run idempotently after all restarts. This is cross-checked by the fixed before-prepare/after-executor boot-identity snapshots showing all four boot IDs changed.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task were satisfied: the inventory web app is running on node2 and node3 (port 8080, verified active and healthy pre- and post-restart), and node1 load-balances HTTP traffic across both backends on port 80 via nginx (verified with repeated sampling showing traffic split across both nodes, both before and after restart). The entire deployment was implemented through an Ansible playbook (site.yml with webapp and loadbalancer roles) executed from the control node (node4), with a successful play recap showing changes applied and idempotently re-verified on a second run. The independent provider-wide restart protocol was also executed correctly on all four managed nodes, each showing a healthy pre-restart baseline, an acknowledged shutdown -r now, a distinct post-restart boot_id, and recovered service/cluster state, cross-confirmed by the fixed before-prepare/after-executor boot-identity snapshots.
limitations: Load-balancing verification relied on grep-based sampling of HTTP response bodies rather than direct nginx access-log inspection, though this is a reasonable and sufficiently reliable proxy for round-robin behavior.

The task instruction did not explicitly specify a load-balancing algorithm (e.g., round-robin vs. least-conn); nginx's default round-robin was used and is a reasonable, unconstrained implementation choice.

sshd on node1-3 was found broken (missing host keys, restart-loop) at task start; this appears to be pre-existing baseline state rather than something introduced by the executor, since the before_prepare snapshot already shows sshd inactive/failing on all three nodes.

operational_hygiene.summary: The executor's troubleshooting mutations (ssh-keygen -A to generate missing host keys, systemctl reset-failed/start ssh on node1-3) were a necessary, bounded prerequisite to establish Ansible SSH connectivity (the nodes shipped with a broken/inactive sshd), not gratuitous experimentation — this is a legitimate corrective action, not an unnecessary mutation. Installing the cluster SSH pubkey to root's authorized_keys on node1-3 (cmd-1f92059d9898428b, cmd-59af34d0aa97456f, cmd-60b570e832ad439c) was required for Ansible connectivity from node4 and is standard practice, not residue. The lifecycle diff confirms no leftover failed services, no unexpected temp-file residue beyond normal per-boot systemd-private dirs, and package-health (dpkg) remained clean on all nodes after executor changes. Removal of node1's default nginx site was an expected and required change for the load-balancer role, not unwanted residue. No destructive, broad, or security-weakening mutations were observed; changes are consistent with expected outcomes of the requested task.
